# Visual Navigation and Visual SLAM {#sec-visual-nav}

The Victoria Park project uses a 2D laser scanner, not a camera. This chapter is
therefore a survey, not an implementation recipe for the project. Its purpose is
to show how the same navigation architecture appears in visual systems:

1. extract repeatable measurements;
2. associate them across time;
3. estimate motion and structure;
4. control drift with loop closure or global measurements.

The sensor changes. The estimation themes do not.

The chapter builds on the camera model and frame conventions of @sec-pnp, keeps
the mathematics compact, and points to the literature for depth. One section is
hands-on: a complete two-view visual odometry example on synthetic data
(@sec-visual-nav-two-view).

## From Images to Motion {#sec-visual-nav-from-images-motion}

Visual navigation starts with image measurements. A camera does not directly
measure range to a tree; it measures pixel intensities. The pipeline must create
geometric constraints from those pixels.

A typical feature-based visual odometry pipeline is:

1. detect image features (or track them from the previous frame);
2. compute descriptors;
3. match features between frames;
4. reject outliers with a geometric model;
5. estimate relative camera motion;
6. triangulate or update map points;
7. decide whether the current frame should become a keyframe.

The result is an incremental trajectory estimate. Without loop closure,
visual odometry drifts just like wheel odometry.

## Camera Model {#sec-visual-nav-camera-model}

@sec-pnp develops the pinhole camera in detail; here is the short version in the
same notation. A world point $\mathbf{p}^w$ maps into the camera's optical frame
($x$ right, $y$ down, $z$ along the optical axis) as
$\mathbf{p}^c = \mathbf{C}_w^c\,\mathbf{p}^w + \mathbf{r}_{cw}^c = [X_c, Y_c, Z_c]^T$,
and then to pixels:

$$
s
\begin{bmatrix}
u \\
v \\
1
\end{bmatrix}
=
\mathbf{K}
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{C}_w^c & \mathbf{r}_{cw}^c
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{p}^w \\
1
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
s = Z_c.
$$ {#eq-visual-nav-projection}

The matrix $[\mathbf{C}_w^c\ \ \mathbf{r}_{cw}^c]$ is the **world-to-camera**
transform, the convention OpenCV uses for `rvec` and `tvec`; the camera's pose in
the world is its inverse (@sec-pnp-problem). The scale factor $s$ is the depth
$Z_c$ of the point in the camera frame. Dividing by it is what makes vision
nonlinear, and what hides absolute scale from a single camera. Two-view geometry
is cleanest in **normalized image coordinates**,
$\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{K}^{-1}[u, v, 1]^T = \mathbf{p}^c / Z_c$, which strip
out the intrinsics.

This is the visual equivalent of a range-bearing sensor model, minus the range.
The measurement function is different, but the estimator still needs a
prediction, a residual, a Jacobian or numerical approximation, and a covariance
(@sec-pnp-covariance-estimation-observation).

## Features and Descriptors {#sec-visual-nav-features-descriptors}

A **detector** finds image locations that are likely to be found again: corners,
blobs, textured patches. A **descriptor** summarizes the local appearance around
each one, so that the same physical point produces a similar descriptor in
another image. A **matcher** proposes correspondences, usually nearest neighbors
in descriptor space, filtered by Lowe's ratio test (keep a match only if the
best candidate is clearly better than the second best) and a mutual-consistency
check.

SIFT [@lowe2004sift] set the standard for invariance to scale and rotation; its
patent expired in 2020 and it now ships with OpenCV. SURF [@bay2008surf] is a
faster approximation. It was patented, and OpenCV still ships it only in a
separately built "nonfree" module, so check its licensing status before using
it in a product. ORB [@rublee2011orb] combines the FAST corner
detector with a rotation-aware binary BRIEF descriptor matched by Hamming
distance at very low cost. It was designed as a free alternative to SIFT and
SURF, and it is the default in real-time systems such as ORB-SLAM. Learned
detectors and descriptors are covered in @sec-visual-nav-learned-front-ends.

### Tracking Instead of Matching {#sec-visual-nav-klt}

At high frame rates a feature barely moves between images, and it is cheaper to
*track* it than to detect and match it again. The Lucas-Kanade tracker
[@lucas1981iterative] assumes brightness constancy,
$I_{k+1}(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{d}) = I_k(\mathbf{u})$, and linearizes it to
$\nabla I^T\mathbf{d} + I_t = 0$: one equation in two unknowns. (That is the
aperture problem. Along a straight edge, only the motion perpendicular to the
edge is observable.) Pooling the equation over a small window $W$ and solving by
least squares gives

$$
\Big(\sum_{W} \nabla I\,\nabla I^T\Big)\,\mathbf{d} = -\sum_{W} \nabla I\, I_t .
$$

The $2 \times 2$ matrix on the left is well conditioned only where the window
contains gradients in two directions, which is exactly what a corner is; Shi and
Tomasi's "good features to track" [@shi1994good] select points where its smaller
eigenvalue is large. Run over an image pyramid to handle larger motions, this
KLT tracker is the front end of VINS-Mono and many other visual-inertial systems.
It is fast and accurate between nearby frames, but tracks drift over long
sequences and a tracker cannot recognize a place it saw an hour ago. That is
still a job for descriptors.

## Two-View Geometry {#sec-visual-nav-two-view-geometry}

Two images of the same points constrain the relative pose of the cameras that
took them. Take camera 1 as the reference and write the relative pose as

$$
\mathbf{p}^{c_2} = \mathbf{C}\,\mathbf{p}^{c_1} + \mathbf{r},
\qquad
\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C}_{c_1}^{c_2},
\qquad
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_{c_2 c_1}^{c_2},
$$

so $\mathbf{r}$ is camera 1's origin as seen from camera 2: the same
world-to-camera form as @eq-visual-nav-projection, with camera 1 playing the
world.

### The Essential Matrix {#sec-visual-nav-essential-matrix}

The vectors $\mathbf{p}^{c_2}$, $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{p}^{c_1}$, and $\mathbf{r}$
are coplanar: they are the sides of the triangle formed by the point and the two
camera centers, all resolved in camera 2. Coplanarity means
$\mathbf{p}^{c_2} \cdot (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{C}\mathbf{p}^{c_1}) = 0$, and
dividing by the two depths gives the **epipolar constraint**

$$
\bar{\mathbf{x}}_2^T\,\mathbf{E}\,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_1 = 0,
\qquad
\mathbf{E} = [\mathbf{r}]_\times\,\mathbf{C}.
$$ {#eq-visual-nav-epipolar}

$\mathbf{E}$ is the **essential matrix**. It has five degrees of freedom (three
for the rotation and two for the direction of $\mathbf{r}$; its overall scale is
meaningless), rank two, and two equal nonzero singular values. In pixel
coordinates the same constraint reads
$\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_2^T\mathbf{F}\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_1 = 0$, with the
**fundamental matrix** $\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{K}^{-T}\mathbf{E}\mathbf{K}^{-1}$,
which is what you estimate when the intrinsics are unknown. Geometrically, a
point in image 1 confines its match in image 2 to a line, the epipolar line. The
check is one-dimensional, so a wrong match that happens to fall near the right
line passes it.

### The Eight-Point and Five-Point Algorithms {#sec-visual-nav-eight-five-point}

Each correspondence gives one equation that is linear in the nine entries of
$\mathbf{E}$. With eight or more, stack them into $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$,
take $\mathbf{e}$ as the right singular vector of $\mathbf{A}$ with the smallest
singular value, and project the result onto valid essential matrices by setting
its singular values to $(1, 1, 0)$. This is the eight-point algorithm of
Longuet-Higgins [@longuethiggins1981]. For the fundamental matrix it works well
only if the pixel coordinates are first normalized to zero mean and unit spread
[@hartley1997defense].

Five correspondences are the minimum. Nistér's five-point algorithm
[@nister2004five] combines them with the cubic constraints every essential
matrix satisfies, $\det\mathbf{E} = 0$ and
$2\mathbf{E}\mathbf{E}^T\mathbf{E} - \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{E}\mathbf{E}^T)\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{0}$,
which leads to a tenth-degree polynomial with up to ten real solutions. It also
works for planar scenes, where the eight-point method degenerates. The main
reason to prefer the minimal solver, though, is RANSAC. Drawing at least one
all-inlier sample of size $m$ with probability $p$, when a fraction $\varepsilon$
of the matches is wrong, takes

$$
N = \frac{\log(1 - p)}{\log\left(1 - (1 - \varepsilon)^m\right)}
$$

samples. With half the matches wrong and $p = 0.99$, five-point samples need
about 145 iterations and eight-point samples about 1200.

### Recovering the Pose {#sec-visual-nav-recovering-pose}

Factor $\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{U}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, 0)\mathbf{V}^T$. With

$$
\mathbf{W} =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & -1 & 0 \\
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix},
$$

the rotation is $\mathbf{U}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{V}^T$ or $\mathbf{U}\mathbf{W}^T\mathbf{V}^T$
(with signs chosen so that the determinant is $+1$), and the translation
direction is $\pm\mathbf{u}_3$, the last column of $\mathbf{U}$
[@hartley2004multiple]. That makes four candidate poses, and only one of them
places the triangulated points in front of both cameras. Testing that, the
**cheirality** check, picks the answer. OpenCV's `cv2.recoverPose` does exactly
this and returns $\mathbf{C}$ and a unit-length $\mathbf{r}$.

### Triangulation {#sec-visual-nav-triangulation}

With the relative pose known, each match fixes a 3D point. View $k$ gives
$\bar{\mathbf{x}}_k \propto \mathbf{P}_k\tilde{\mathbf{p}}$, with
$\tilde{\mathbf{p}} = [\mathbf{p}^{c_1}; 1]$,
$\mathbf{P}_1 = [\mathbf{I}\ \ \mathbf{0}]$, and
$\mathbf{P}_2 = [\mathbf{C}\ \ \mathbf{r}]$ (multiply by $\mathbf{K}$ to work in
pixels). The cross product
$\bar{\mathbf{x}}_k \times (\mathbf{P}_k\tilde{\mathbf{p}}) = \mathbf{0}$
contributes two independent linear equations per view, and the resulting
$4 \times 4$ homogeneous system is solved by SVD. This direct linear transform
(DLT) is what `cv2.triangulatePoints` implements [@hartley2004multiple].

Its precision depends on parallax. For two cameras a baseline $b$ apart and
looking the same way, depth comes from the disparity $d = f b / Z$, so

$$
\sigma_Z \approx \frac{Z^2}{f\,b}\,\sigma_d .
$$

Depth error grows with the square of the range and shrinks only linearly with
the baseline. A pair of frames with little parallax gives depth that is mostly
noise, which is why keyframes are chosen for parallax
(@sec-visual-nav-keyframes-bundle-adjustment).

### Scale {#sec-visual-nav-scale-ambiguity}

Multiply every point and the translation by the same $\lambda > 0$:
$\mathbf{C}(\lambda\mathbf{p}^{c_1}) + \lambda\mathbf{r} = \lambda\,\mathbf{p}^{c_2}$.
Projection divides by depth, so every pixel in both images is unchanged. Two
images determine the translation only up to scale, which is why `recoverPose`
returns a unit vector. A single camera cannot tell a model railway filmed from
30 cm away from the real railway filmed from a helicopter.

## Geometry Checks {#sec-visual-nav-geometry-checks}

Raw descriptor matches are not trustworthy. They need geometric verification:

- **Essential matrix:** calibrated two-view motion up to scale
  (@sec-visual-nav-essential-matrix).
- **Fundamental matrix:** uncalibrated two-view epipolar geometry.
- **Homography:** a planar scene, or a camera that only rotates.
- **PnP:** camera pose from known 3D points and 2D image observations
  (@sec-pnp).
- **RANSAC:** robustly fit any of these while rejecting outliers
  [@fischler1981ransac].

This is the visual analog of statistical gating in landmark SLAM
(@sec-slam-association-innovation-mahalanobis-distance). The details are
different, but the goal is identical: keep bad correspondences from entering the
estimator.

## Two-View Visual Odometry by Hand {#sec-visual-nav-two-view}

Here is the whole two-view pipeline on synthetic data, using the camera model
and conventions of @sec-pnp. A camera at the origin and a second camera 1.5 m
to its right (a little forward and slightly rotated; think of a survey drone
sliding along a building facade) both look at 200 points between 4 and 12 m
away. Feature positions get 0.5 px of noise, and 20% of the matches are replaced
by garbage, a realistic rate for raw descriptor matching. Variable names follow
the book's subscript-first habit: `C_c1_c2` is $\mathbf{C}_{c_1}^{c_2}$ and
`r_c2c1_c2` is $\mathbf{r}_{c_2c_1}^{c_2}$.

::: {#visual-nav-two-view-setup .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import cv2
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# A generic VGA camera; optical frame: x right, y down, z along the optical axis.
K = np.array([[500.0, 0.0, 320.0],
              [0.0, 500.0, 240.0],
              [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]])
WIDTH, HEIGHT = 640, 480


def project(K, p_c):
    """Pinhole projection of (N, 3) camera-frame points to (N, 2) pixels."""
    uvw = (K @ p_c.T).T
    return uvw[:, :2] / uvw[:, 2:3]


rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

# Scene: 200 points 4 to 12 m in front of camera 1, whose frame serves as the world.
n_points = 200
p_c1 = np.column_stack([rng.uniform(-5.0, 5.0, n_points),
                        rng.uniform(-3.0, 3.0, n_points),
                        rng.uniform(4.0, 12.0, n_points)])

# Camera 2: 1.5 m right, 0.1 m up (y is down), 0.3 m forward, rotated by a few degrees.
r_c1c2_c1 = np.array([1.5, -0.1, 0.3])                 # camera 2's position in camera 1 axes
C_c2_c1, _ = cv2.Rodrigues(np.deg2rad(np.array([1.0, -4.0, 0.5])))
C_c1_c2 = C_c2_c1.T                                    # camera 1 coordinates -> camera 2
r_c2c1_c2 = -C_c1_c2 @ r_c1c2_c1                       # camera 1's origin, seen from camera 2
p_c2 = (C_c1_c2 @ p_c1.T).T + r_c2c1_c2


def in_image(uv):
    return np.all((uv > 0) & (uv < [WIDTH, HEIGHT]), axis=1)


# Pixels in both images; keep points both cameras see, add noise and 20% bad matches.
uv1_true, uv2_true = project(K, p_c1), project(K, p_c2)
visible = in_image(uv1_true) & in_image(uv2_true)
p_c1, uv1_true, uv2_true = p_c1[visible], uv1_true[visible], uv2_true[visible]
n = len(p_c1)
uv1 = uv1_true + rng.normal(0.0, 0.5, (n, 2))          # 0.5 px feature noise
uv2 = uv2_true + rng.normal(0.0, 0.5, (n, 2))
bad_match = rng.random(n) < 0.2
uv2[bad_match] = rng.uniform([0, 0], [WIDTH, HEIGHT], (bad_match.sum(), 2))
print(f"{n} matches visible in both images, {bad_match.sum()} of them wrong")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
155 matches visible in both images, 30 of them wrong
```
:::
:::


Now estimate $\mathbf{E}$ robustly and recover the pose. OpenCV's
`USAC_ACCURATE` method is RANSAC around the five-point solver, plus a
local-optimization step that re-fits the model to the current inliers; plain
`cv2.RANSAC` keeps the model from the best minimal sample without re-fitting and
is noticeably less accurate on this example (swap the flag and see). The
threshold is the largest acceptable distance, in pixels, from a point to its
epipolar line.

::: {#visual-nav-two-view-essential .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
E, ransac_mask = cv2.findEssentialMat(uv1, uv2, K, method=cv2.USAC_ACCURATE,
                                      prob=0.999, threshold=1.5)
inlier = ransac_mask.ravel().astype(bool)
print(f"RANSAC kept {inlier.sum()} matches ({np.sum(inlier & ~bad_match)} good,"
      f" {np.sum(inlier & bad_match)} bad) and rejected {np.sum(~inlier)}"
      f" ({np.sum(~inlier & ~bad_match)} of them good)")

# Pose from E: four candidates, cheirality picks one. Returns C_c1^c2 and a unit t.
n_in_front, C_est, t_est, _ = cv2.recoverPose(E, uv1, uv2, K, mask=ransac_mask.copy())
t_est = t_est.ravel()
rotation_error = np.rad2deg(np.linalg.norm(cv2.Rodrigues(C_est @ C_c1_c2.T)[0]))
t_true_unit = r_c2c1_c2 / np.linalg.norm(r_c2c1_c2)
direction_error = np.rad2deg(np.arccos(np.clip(t_est @ t_true_unit, -1.0, 1.0)))
print(f"rotation error {rotation_error:.2f} deg, translation direction error"
      f" {direction_error:.2f} deg")
print(f"|t| = {np.linalg.norm(t_est):.3f}, but the true baseline is"
      f" {np.linalg.norm(r_c2c1_c2):.3f} m")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
RANSAC kept 124 matches (124 good, 0 bad) and rejected 31 (1 of them good)
rotation error 0.13 deg, translation direction error 0.19 deg
|t| = 1.000, but the true baseline is 1.533 m
```
:::
:::


To see the cheirality check at work, decompose $\mathbf{E}$ into its four
candidate poses, triangulate the inliers with each, and count the points that
land in front of both cameras. The `triangulate` helper is the DLT of
@sec-visual-nav-triangulation, through OpenCV.

::: {#visual-nav-two-view-cheirality .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def triangulate(C, t, uv1, uv2):
    """DLT triangulation in camera 1's frame, with camera 2 at [C | t]."""
    P1 = K @ np.hstack([np.eye(3), np.zeros((3, 1))])
    P2 = K @ np.column_stack([C, t])
    p_h = cv2.triangulatePoints(P1, P2, uv1.T.astype(float), uv2.T.astype(float))
    return (p_h[:3] / p_h[3]).T


C_a, C_b, t_svd = cv2.decomposeEssentialMat(E)
for name, C, t in [("C_a, +t", C_a, t_svd), ("C_a, -t", C_a, -t_svd),
                   ("C_b, +t", C_b, t_svd), ("C_b, -t", C_b, -t_svd)]:
    p = triangulate(C, t.ravel(), uv1[inlier], uv2[inlier])
    depth_1, depth_2 = p[:, 2], (p @ C.T + t.ravel())[:, 2]
    n_front = np.sum((depth_1 > 0) & (depth_2 > 0))
    print(f"candidate {name}: {n_front:3d} of {inlier.sum()} points in front of both cameras")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
candidate C_a, +t:   0 of 124 points in front of both cameras
candidate C_a, -t:   0 of 124 points in front of both cameras
candidate C_b, +t:   0 of 124 points in front of both cameras
candidate C_b, -t: 124 of 124 points in front of both cameras
```
:::
:::


Finally, triangulate with the recovered pose and confront the scale.

::: {#visual-nav-two-view-scale .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
p_est = triangulate(C_est, t_est, uv1[inlier], uv2[inlier])   # in units of the baseline
p_true = p_c1[inlier]
baseline = np.linalg.norm(r_c2c1_c2)
scale_fit = np.sum(p_est * p_true) / np.sum(p_est * p_est)     # least-squares scale
error = np.linalg.norm(baseline * p_est - p_true, axis=1)
print(f"best-fit scale {scale_fit:.3f}; true baseline {baseline:.3f} m")
print(f"after scaling by the true baseline: median 3D error {np.median(error):.2f} m,"
      f" max {error.max():.2f} m")

# The scale ambiguity in two lines: a world three times larger gives identical pixels.
lam = 3.0
uv2_big = project(K, (C_c1_c2 @ (lam * p_c1).T).T + lam * r_c2c1_c2)
print(f"largest pixel change with scene and baseline scaled by {lam:.0f}:"
      f" {np.abs(uv2_big - uv2_true).max():.1e} px")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
best-fit scale 1.510; true baseline 1.533 m
after scaling by the true baseline: median 3D error 0.12 m, max 0.38 m
largest pixel change with scene and baseline scaled by 3: 1.4e-13 px
```
:::
:::


::: {#cell-fig-visual-nav-two-view .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.15, 1]})

ax = axes[0]
flow = uv2 - uv1
ax.quiver(uv1[inlier, 0], uv1[inlier, 1], flow[inlier, 0], flow[inlier, 1], angles="xy",
          scale_units="xy", scale=1, color="C0", width=0.003, label="kept by RANSAC")
ax.quiver(uv1[~inlier, 0], uv1[~inlier, 1], flow[~inlier, 0], flow[~inlier, 1], angles="xy",
          scale_units="xy", scale=1, color="C3", width=0.002, alpha=0.6, label="rejected")
ax.set_xlim(0, WIDTH)
ax.set_ylim(HEIGHT, 0)                                   # image rows grow downward
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlabel("u [px]")
ax.set_ylabel("v [px]")
ax.set_title("(a) feature motion between the two images")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8)

ax = axes[1]
camera2_unit = -C_est.T @ t_est                          # camera 2 center in camera 1 axes
ax.scatter(p_true[:, 0], p_true[:, 2], s=28, facecolors="none", edgecolors="0.55",
           label="truth")
ax.scatter(p_est[:, 0], p_est[:, 2], s=8, color="C1", label="triangulated, |t| = 1")
ax.scatter(baseline * p_est[:, 0], baseline * p_est[:, 2], s=8, color="C0",
           label="scaled by the true baseline")
ax.plot([0.0, camera2_unit[0], baseline * camera2_unit[0]],
        [0.0, camera2_unit[2], baseline * camera2_unit[2]], "^", color="black", markersize=8)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlabel("x (right) [m]")
ax.set_ylabel("z (forward) [m]")
ax.set_title("(b) reconstruction, top view")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.25)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

From noisy pixels with a fifth of the matches wrong, the rotation and the
translation direction both come back to within a few tenths of a degree. The
four-candidate printout shows why the cheirality check is not optional: the
wrong candidates fit the epipolar constraint exactly as well as the right one,
and only the depth signs tell them apart. The translation, though, has length 1
by construction, and the triangulated points come out in units of the baseline.
Scaled by the true baseline of 1.53 m they land on the truth; without that number, nothing in
the images distinguishes this reconstruction from one three times larger, as the
last printout shows to machine precision. Chaining such estimates frame after
frame is monocular visual odometry, and each link both inherits and perturbs the
scale of the one before (@sec-visual-nav-scale-drift).

## Keyframes and Bundle Adjustment {#sec-visual-nav-keyframes-bundle-adjustment}

Chaining two-view estimates accumulates error quickly, so visual odometry systems
keep a sparse set of **keyframes** and refine them jointly. A new keyframe is
inserted when the camera has moved far enough to give useful parallax, or when
the number of tracked features drops below a threshold. Frames in between are
tracked against the existing map points with PnP (@sec-pnp) but not stored.
PTAM [@klein2007ptam] introduced the split between a fast tracking thread and a
slower mapping thread that optimizes keyframes, and nearly every later system
inherits it.

The optimization is **bundle adjustment** (BA): adjust all keyframe poses and
point positions to minimize the total reprojection error,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\min_{\{\mathbf{C}_w^{c_j},\,\mathbf{r}_{c_j w}^{c_j}\},\,\{\mathbf{p}_i^w\}}
\ \sum_{j}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}(j)}
\rho\left(\mathbf{e}_{ij}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u^{-1}\mathbf{e}_{ij}\right), \\
&\mathbf{e}_{ij} = \mathbf{u}_{ij} - \pi\left(\mathbf{K},\ \mathbf{C}_w^{c_j}\mathbf{p}_i^w + \mathbf{r}_{c_j w}^{c_j}\right),
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-visual-nav-bundle-adjustment}

where $\mathcal{V}(j)$ is the set of points seen in keyframe $j$,
$\mathbf{u}_{ij}$ is the observation of point $i$ in keyframe $j$, $\pi$ is the
projection of @eq-visual-nav-projection, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u$ is the pixel
noise covariance, and $\rho$ is a robust kernel
(@sec-loop-closure-robust-kernels). It is the pose graph's bigger sibling: the
same sparse nonlinear least squares, with the points as variables too
[@triggs2000].

The structure is what makes it tractable. Every residual involves one camera and
one point, so in the Gauss-Newton normal equations the camera-camera block
$\mathbf{H}_{cc}$ and the point-point block $\mathbf{H}_{pp}$ are both block
diagonal ($6 \times 6$ per keyframe, $3 \times 3$ per point), and all of the
coupling lives in $\mathbf{H}_{cp}$. Eliminating the points with the Schur
complement leaves the much smaller **reduced camera system**

$$
\left(\mathbf{H}_{cc} - \mathbf{H}_{cp}\mathbf{H}_{pp}^{-1}\mathbf{H}_{pc}\right)\Delta\mathbf{c}
= -\mathbf{g}_c + \mathbf{H}_{cp}\mathbf{H}_{pp}^{-1}\mathbf{g}_p ,
$$ {#eq-visual-nav-schur}

which is solved for the camera updates $\Delta\mathbf{c}$. Each point's update
then follows on its own,
$\Delta\mathbf{p}_i = -\mathbf{H}_{p_i p_i}^{-1}(\mathbf{g}_{p_i} + \mathbf{H}_{p_i c}\Delta\mathbf{c})$.
Inverting $\mathbf{H}_{pp}$ costs one $3 \times 3$ inverse per point, so a
problem with 500 keyframes and 50,000 points becomes a $3000 \times 3000$ linear
system instead of a $153{,}000 \times 153{,}000$ one
(@sec-math-reference-bundle-adjustment-mathematics works through the details).
Real-time systems run local BA over a sliding window of recent keyframes and
marginalize the older ones; global BA, or a pose graph as in @sec-loop-closure,
runs after a loop closure.

## Monocular Scale and Scale Drift {#sec-visual-nav-scale-drift}

A monocular system fixes the scale arbitrarily at initialization, typically by
declaring the first baseline to have unit length or the median scene depth to be
one. Later frames inherit that scale through the map: each new pose comes from
PnP against points that carry the old scale, and each new point is triangulated
from poses that carry it too. Small errors in the hand-off compound
multiplicatively, so the scale itself random-walks along the trajectory. This is
**scale drift**. After a long excursion the trajectory can have a good shape but
be several percent too small or too large, and a loop closure must then correct a
similarity transform (seven degrees of freedom in 3D: rotation, translation, and
scale) rather than a rigid one [@strasdat2010scale]. Monocular ORB-SLAM closes
loops in $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ for exactly this reason.

Every practical fix brings in a metric measurement from outside the images: a
stereo baseline, an IMU's accelerometers, wheel odometry, a known camera height
above a ground plane, an altimeter, GNSS, or an object of known size. Project 1
gets scale for free from the known size of the AprilTags (@sec-pnp).

## Visual Odometry vs. Visual SLAM {#sec-visual-nav-odometry-visual-slam}

Visual odometry estimates motion incrementally. Visual SLAM adds a persistent map
and loop closure.

| System | Keeps map? | Uses loop closure? | Typical output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Visual odometry | local only | no | drifting trajectory |
| Visual SLAM | yes | yes | trajectory plus reusable map |
| Visual-inertial odometry | local only | usually no | metric short-term trajectory |
| Visual-inertial SLAM | yes | yes | metric trajectory and map |

The distinction matters because many impressive demos are odometry demos.
Long-term autonomy requires handling drift.

## ORB-SLAM as a Reference Architecture {#sec-visual-nav-orb-slam-as}

ORB-SLAM [@murartal2015orbslam] is a useful reference system because it separates
the work into threads:

- **Tracking:** estimate the current camera pose from recent map points.
- **Local mapping:** add keyframes and map points, and run local bundle
  adjustment.
- **Loop closing:** detect revisited places with a bag of words, verify them,
  and correct drift with a pose-graph optimization (@sec-loop-closure); later
  versions follow it with a global bundle adjustment.

That architecture mirrors the course project:

- feature extraction from laser scans;
- local data association against tree landmarks;
- FastSLAM back end;
- written analysis of loop closure limitations.

Students are not expected to implement ORB-SLAM in this module. The point is to
recognize the recurring system pattern.

## Direct and Semi-Direct Methods {#sec-visual-nav-direct-methods}

Feature-based methods throw away most of the image and keep only keypoints.
**Direct** methods skip features and minimize a photometric error instead: take
a pixel $\mathbf{u}$ with depth $d_{\mathbf{u}}$ in a reference frame,
back-project it, move it with the candidate relative pose $\mathbf{T}_r^k$,
project it into the current frame, and compare intensities,

$$
r_{\mathbf{u}} = I_k\Big(\pi\big(\mathbf{T}_r^k\,\pi^{-1}(\mathbf{u}, d_{\mathbf{u}})\big)\Big) - I_r(\mathbf{u}),
$$

summed over many pixels with strong gradients. LSD-SLAM [@engel2014lsd] tracks
semi-dense depth maps on all high-gradient pixels and closes loops with a
$\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ pose graph. DSO [@engel2018dso] jointly optimizes a sparse set
of pixels, poses, and inverse depths over a sliding window, and models the
camera's exposure time, vignetting, and response curve, without which brightness
constancy is a polite fiction. SVO [@forster2014svo] is semi-direct: direct
alignment for fast tracking, features for mapping, built for the tight compute
budget of small aerial vehicles. Direct methods exploit edges and weak texture
that detectors ignore and can be very accurate with a well-calibrated camera.
They are more sensitive to lighting changes, rolling-shutter distortion, and poor
initialization, and they need small motion between frames because the
photometric cost is only locally convex.

## Visual-Inertial Odometry {#sec-visual-nav-vio}

Cameras and IMUs fail in complementary ways
(@sec-advanced-slam-visual-inertial-odometry has a table). The IMU measures
specific force and angular rate at hundreds of hertz, in metric units, with
gravity mixed in; it carries the estimate through blur, darkness, and fast motion,
but its biases make it drift within seconds to minutes. The camera bounds that
drift by tracking the environment. Together they make scale observable, and
gravity gives roll and pitch. Two ideas carry most modern VIO systems, and one
piece of theory explains their limits.

### MSCKF: Features Without Landmarks {#sec-visual-nav-msckf}

The multi-state constraint Kalman filter (MSCKF) [@mourikis2007msckf] is an
error-state EKF (@sec-ekf-error-state-filtering) whose state holds the current
IMU state (attitude, velocity, position, and gyro and accelerometer biases) plus
a sliding window of "clones" of recent camera poses. Features are *not* in the
state. When a feature track ends, the filter triangulates the feature from the
clones that saw it and linearizes the stacked reprojection residuals of all $M$
observations:

$$
\mathbf{r} \approx \mathbf{H}_x\,\delta\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{H}_f\,\delta\mathbf{p}_f + \mathbf{n},
$$ {#eq-visual-nav-msckf}

where $\delta\mathbf{x}$ is the state error and $\delta\mathbf{p}_f$ the error in
the triangulated feature position. $\mathbf{H}_f$ has $2M$ rows and 3 columns.
Let the $2M - 3$ orthonormal columns of $\mathbf{N}$ span its left null space, so
$\mathbf{N}^T\mathbf{H}_f = \mathbf{0}$. Multiplying through by $\mathbf{N}^T$
removes the feature entirely,

$$
\mathbf{r}_o = \mathbf{N}^T\mathbf{r} \approx \mathbf{N}^T\mathbf{H}_x\,\delta\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{N}^T\mathbf{n},
$$

leaving $2M - 3$ residuals that constrain only the IMU state and camera clones,
ready for a standard EKF update. The cost is linear in the number of features,
and no feature ever enters the covariance. The same projection works in a
sigma-point filter (@sec-ukf), but the EKF form is the classic one.

### IMU Preintegration {#sec-visual-nav-preintegration}

Optimization-based VIO puts IMU measurements into a factor graph alongside
reprojection residuals. There are hundreds of IMU samples between keyframes, and
integrating them forward from the state at keyframe $i$ would have to be redone
every time the optimizer moved that state. **Preintegration**
[@lupton2012visual; @forster2017preintegration] integrates them once, in the body
frame of keyframe $i$, into relative increments that do not depend on the global
state. Write $\bar{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_k = \tilde{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_{ib,k}^b - \mathbf{b}_g$
and $\bar{\mathbf{f}}_k = \tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{ib,k}^b - \mathbf{b}_a$ for the
gyro and specific-force samples corrected by the current bias estimates, and
$\Delta t$ for the IMU sample interval. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\mathbf{C}_{ij} &= \prod_{k=i}^{j-1}\operatorname{Exp}\left(\bar{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_k\,\Delta t\right), \\
\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ij} &= \sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Delta\mathbf{C}_{ik}\,\bar{\mathbf{f}}_k\,\Delta t, \\
\Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij} &= \sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\left[\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ik}\,\Delta t + \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta\mathbf{C}_{ik}\,\bar{\mathbf{f}}_k\,\Delta t^2\right].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-visual-nav-preintegration}

With $\mathbf{C}_i = \mathbf{C}_{b_i}^n$, gravity $\mathbf{g}^n$, the interval
$\Delta t_{ij}$ between the keyframes, and Earth rotation neglected, the
keyframe states are related by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{C}_j &= \mathbf{C}_i\,\Delta\mathbf{C}_{ij}, \\
\mathbf{v}_j &= \mathbf{v}_i + \mathbf{g}^n\Delta t_{ij} + \mathbf{C}_i\,\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ij}, \\
\mathbf{p}_j &= \mathbf{p}_i + \mathbf{v}_i\,\Delta t_{ij} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{g}^n\Delta t_{ij}^2 + \mathbf{C}_i\,\Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij},
\end{aligned}
$$

and those three equations become a single factor between keyframes $i$ and $j$.
The increments depend on the biases, so implementations store their first-order
Jacobians with respect to $\mathbf{b}_g$ and $\mathbf{b}_a$ and correct the
increments when the bias estimates change, instead of reintegrating. Lupton and
Sukkarieh developed the idea at the Australian Centre for Field Robotics, the
same lab that recorded the Victoria Park dataset.

### Unobservable Directions {#sec-visual-nav-vio-observability}

Some things no VIO system can know. Shift the whole trajectory and every
landmark by a constant offset, or rotate everything about the gravity vector, and
every image and every IMU sample is unchanged: the accelerometers sense gravity,
which fixes "down," but nothing fixes north or the origin. VIO therefore has
**four unobservable directions**, global position (three) and yaw about gravity
(one) [@hesch2014consistency]. Roll and pitch are observable through gravity,
and scale through the accelerometers, given enough excitation; motion at
constant velocity hides the scale again. This is the observability analysis of
@sec-kf-observability with real consequences. An EKF that relinearizes at
changing estimates can acquire spurious information along yaw and become
confident about a direction it cannot possibly know; first-estimates Jacobians
[@huang2010] and observability-constrained EKFs [@hesch2014consistency] restore
the correct null space. It is also why VINS-Mono's loop-closure pose graph has
four degrees of freedom per keyframe rather than six: roll and pitch are already
pinned by gravity. Over the long term a VIO system needs GNSS, a map, or a
magnetometer to fix what it cannot see, a theme @sec-ins-gnss develops for
inertial navigation in general.

## Visual-Inertial Systems in Practice {#sec-visual-nav-vi-systems}

Three open systems are worth knowing by name. ORB-SLAM3 [@campos2021orbslam3]
extends the ORB-SLAM architecture to monocular, stereo, and RGB-D cameras,
pinhole and fisheye lenses, and tight visual-inertial fusion with preintegrated
IMU factors, and it keeps an "atlas" of disconnected maps that merge when a place
is recognized across them. VINS-Mono [@qin2018vins] pairs a KLT front end with a
sliding-window optimizer over preintegrated IMU factors and reprojection
residuals, includes a careful initialization that recovers scale, gravity, and
biases from the first seconds of motion, and closes loops with DBoW2 and its
four-degree-of-freedom pose graph. OpenVINS [@geneva2020openvins] is a research
platform built on the MSCKF, with first-estimates Jacobians, online camera-IMU
calibration including the time offset, and good evaluation tools; it is the
easiest of the three to read alongside this chapter.

## Learned Front Ends {#sec-visual-nav-learned-front-ends}

Deep networks have entered visual navigation mostly through the front end.
SuperPoint [@detone2018superpoint] outputs keypoints and descriptors in a single
pass and is trained without manual labels by warping images with known
homographies. LightGlue [@lindenberger2023lightglue] replaces nearest-neighbor
matching with an attention-based network that reasons about all keypoints of both
images together, and stops early on easy image pairs. Together they are far more
robust than ORB to large changes in viewpoint and illumination. DROID-SLAM
[@teed2021droid] goes further: a recurrent network iteratively refines dense
optical flow between frames, and a differentiable dense bundle adjustment layer
turns the flow into poses and depths, giving remarkable robustness at the price
of a substantial GPU. Notice what did not change. The networks produce
correspondences, and geometry (RANSAC, triangulation, bundle adjustment) still
turns them into navigation. @sec-advanced-slam-learning-based-emerging surveys the
wider landscape.

## Monocular, Stereo, RGB-D, and Visual-Inertial {#sec-visual-nav-monocular-stereo-rgb}

Different camera setups provide different observability:

| Sensor setup | Scale observable? | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| monocular | no, without extra information | cheap and light | scale ambiguity and drift |
| stereo | yes | direct depth from disparity | needs baseline and texture |
| RGB-D | yes | dense short-range depth | limited outdoor range |
| visual-inertial | yes after initialization | robust short-term motion | calibration and timing sensitive |

This connects directly to the broader navigation course: inertial sensing often
supplies short-term motion constraints, while vision supplies environmental
corrections.

## What Carries Over to Victoria Park {#sec-visual-nav-what-carries-over}

The project is laser-based, but several visual-SLAM lessons carry over:

- front-end quality controls back-end quality;
- association failures are estimator failures;
- outlier rejection is not optional;
- loop closure needs both recognition and geometric consistency;
- diagnostic plots matter more than a pretty final map.

In Victoria Park, the "features" are tree trunks instead of image keypoints. The
conceptual pipeline is the same.

## Summary {#sec-visual-nav-summary}

Visual navigation broadens the SLAM picture without changing the core estimation
questions. Cameras create bearing-only geometric constraints; lidar tree features
create range-bearing landmark constraints. Both systems must solve measurement
modeling, association, drift, and loop closure. The visual specifics are worth
remembering: the essential matrix and RANSAC turn matches into relative pose up
to scale, triangulation needs parallax, bundle adjustment is sparse nonlinear
least squares made tractable by the Schur complement, monocular scale must come
from somewhere else, and VIO gets scale, roll, and pitch from the IMU but can
never see global position or yaw.

For the project, use this chapter as survey context. Do not turn it into a second
implementation burden.

## Exercises {#sec-visual-nav-exercises}

1. **The epipolar constraint.** (a) Derive @eq-visual-nav-epipolar from the
   coplanarity of $\mathbf{p}^{c_2}$, $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{p}^{c_1}$, and
   $\mathbf{r}$. (b) Show that $\mathbf{E}$ has rank two with two equal nonzero
   singular values. (Hint: find the singular values of $[\mathbf{r}]_\times$, and
   remember that $\mathbf{C}$ is orthogonal.) (c) Explain why $\mathbf{E}$ has
   five degrees of freedom and why five correspondences are the minimum.
   (d) Show that $\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{K}^{-T}\mathbf{E}\mathbf{K}^{-1}$.

2. **A hovering drone that only yaws.** Set the translation in the two-view
   example to zero, as for a multirotor yawing in place. (a) Run
   `cv2.findEssentialMat` and `cv2.recoverPose`. What do you get, and why is
   @eq-visual-nav-epipolar useless here? (b) Show that for pure rotation the
   pixels are related by the homography $\mathbf{K}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{K}^{-1}$,
   estimate it with `cv2.findHomography`, and recover $\mathbf{C}$. (c) How
   should a visual odometry front end detect this situation, and what should it
   do about keyframes and triangulation while it lasts?

3. **Parallax buys depth.** In the two-view example, sweep the baseline from
   0.05 m to 3 m (keep its direction). For each baseline, record the rotation
   error, the translation direction error, and the median triangulation error
   after scaling by the true baseline. Plot them against the baseline and compare
   the depth error with $\sigma_Z \approx Z^2\sigma_d/(fb)$, taking
   $\sigma_d = \sqrt{2} \times 0.5$ px and $Z$ the median depth. What minimum
   baseline would you require before inserting a keyframe?

4. **Scale drift on a pipeline survey.** A monocular camera on an inspection
   drone flies 2 km along a straight pipeline, inserting a keyframe every 5 m.
   At each keyframe the scale is handed off with a 1% random error,
   $s_k = s_{k-1}(1 + \varepsilon_k)$ with $\varepsilon_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.01^2)$.
   (a) Simulate 1000 flights and plot the spread of $s_k$ against $k$; compare
   it with $0.01\sqrt{k}$. (b) Derive the one-sigma along-track position error
   at the end of the flight to first order in $\varepsilon$, and check it against
   the simulation. (c) The drone flies back and recognizes its launch point.
   Explain why a rigid $SE(3)$ correction cannot remove the error and a
   $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ correction can.

5. **What VIO cannot see.** (a) Show that adding a constant offset to every
   position (trajectory and landmarks), or rotating the whole scene and
   trajectory about the gravity vector, leaves every accelerometer, gyro, and
   camera measurement unchanged. (b) Show that a rotation about a horizontal
   axis does change the accelerometer measurements, so roll and pitch are
   observable. (c) A VIO-equipped drone flies for ten minutes without GNSS. Which
   parts of its navigation solution would you trust, and which would you expect
   to have drifted? (d) Why does VINS-Mono use a four-degree-of-freedom pose
   graph for loop closure?

6. **Schur complement bookkeeping.** A bundle adjustment problem has $m = 500$
   keyframes and $n = 50{,}000$ points, and each point is seen by 8 keyframes on
   average. (a) Derive @eq-visual-nav-schur and the back-substitution for
   $\Delta\mathbf{p}_i$ from the block normal equations. (b) Give the dimensions
   of $\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{H}_{pp}$, and the reduced camera system, and
   estimate the number of nonzero entries of $\mathbf{H}_{cp}$. (c) Why are the
   points eliminated rather than the cameras? (d) When is the reduced camera
   system sparse, and when does it become dense?
